To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

quiescent radial-glia (qRG) are not activated after injury in the adult zebrafish midbrain tectal plate, but that neuro-epithelium-like (NE) cells in the internal marginal zone proliferate and give rise to neurogenic progeny.

quiescent RG in the zebrabrafish midbrain tectal have limited regenerative capacity, but that homeostatic neuro-epithelium-like stem/progenitor populations can be recruited to amplify regenerative neurogenesis after brain injury.

(1) qRG in the zebrabish midbrain tectal plate have limited regenerative capacity, (2) injury amplifies the regenerative potential of homeostatic NE progenitors in the tectal marginal zones and (3) Wnt/βcatenin signalling regulates regenerative neurogenesis in the internal tectal zone.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms that control tissue regeneration in the adult brain.
the mechanisms underlying tissue repair following damage in adult zebrafish.
how stem and progenitor cell populations in the zebrahfi brain respond to injury and how this is regulated by Wnt signalling.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
quiescent RG are not a major player in tissue regeneration after injury in the tectal midbrain of adult zebrafish.
the RG are heterogeneous and have different functions.
the quiescent RG are not the main source of regeneration in the tectal region, and the neuroepithelial progenitor cells are the main contributors of regeneration.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the tectal qRG have a limited regenerative potential, but the tectal NE stem cells have an increased regenerative capacity.
the tectum is composed of a diverse population of stem cells, and that homeostatic growth is the main mechanism for regeneration.
the tectal qRG have a restricted regenerative capacity, but the tectal NE progenitors can be activated to compensate for the injury by amplifying neurogenesis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
quiescent RG in the zebrabish brain have restricted regenerative capacities and are not a primary source of neurogenesis following injury.
not all RG act the same during regeneration and that the regenerative capacity of stem/progenitor populations is highly context-dependent.
quiescent RG do not contribute to neuronal repair post-injury.
